title: Station wagon
description: Auto body style with its roof extended rearward
wiki_lead:
A station wagon (US, also wagon) or estate car (UK, also estate) is an automotive body-style variant of a sedan with its roof extended rearward over a shared passenger/cargo volume with access at the back via a third or fifth door (the liftgate, or tailgate), instead of a trunk/boot lid. The body style transforms a standard three-box design into a two-box design, to include an A, B, and C-pillar, as well as a D-pillar. Station wagons can flexibly reconfigure their interior volume via fold-down rear seats to prioritize either passenger or cargo volume.
The American Heritage Dictionary defines a station wagon as "an automobile with one or more rows of folding or removable seats behind the driver and no luggage compartment but an area behind the seats into which suitcases, parcels, etc., can be loaded through a tailgate."
When a model range includes multiple body styles, such as sedan, hatchback, and station wagon, the models typically share their platform, drivetrain, and bodywork forward of the A-pillar, and usually the B-pillar. In 1969, Popular Mechanics said, "Station wagon-style ... follows that of the production sedan of which it is the counterpart. Most are on the same wheelbase, offer the same transmission and engine options, and the same comfort and convenience options."
Station wagons have evolved from their early use as specialized vehicles to carry people and luggage to and from a train station. The demand for station wagon body style has faded since the 2010s in favor of the crossover or SUV designs, especially in the United States and Canada.

Name

Reflecting the original purpose of transporting people and luggage between country estates and railway stations, the station wagon body style is called an "estate car" or "estate" in the United Kingdom or a "wagon" in Australia and New Zealand.
Either horse-drawn or automotive, the earliest use of the station wagon description would be considered to describe utility vehicles or light trucks. The depot hackney or taxi, often on a Model T chassis with an exposed wood body, most often found around railroad stations, was the predecessor of the station wagon body style in the United States. These early models with exposed wooden bodies became known as woodies. By the 1920s the status of the station wagon description changed to consider them as vehicles for passengers.
In Germany, the term "kombi" is used.
This is short for Kombinationskraftwagen ("combination motor vehicle"). "Kombi" is also the term used in Poland.
In Russia and some post-Soviet countries, this type of car is called "universal".
Manufacturers may designate station wagons across various model lines with a proprietary nameplate for marketing and advertising differentiation. Examples include "Avant", "Break", "Caravan", "Kombi", "Sports Tourer", "Sports Wagon", "Tourer", "Touring", and "Variant".

grok_lead: A station wagon is an automobile with a body style featuring an extended passenger compartment that reaches to the rear of the vehicle, lacking a separate trunk but including one or more rows of foldable or removable seats behind the driver and a tailgate that opens at the rear for easy access to cargo space. This design distinguishes it from sedans and hatchbacks, emphasizing versatility for transporting both passenger s and luggage, and it falls under the federal classification of passenger cars manufactured primarily for carrying people, including those equipped for towing light trailers. The term "station wagon" originated in the 19th century, referring to horse-drawn carriages used to transport passengers and goods to and from railroad stations, evolving into early 20th-century motorized versions known as "depot hacks" or "carryalls." The first production automobiles fitting this style appeared in the 1920s, such as the 1923 Star model and the 1929 Ford Model A, typically built with wooden bodies on commercial chassis by third-party manufacturers for use around train depots or rural estates. These early wagons were expensive, low-volume vehicles often classified as commercial rather than passenger cars, with wood-paneled "woody" designs providing durability for hauling people and cargo. By the 1930s, major automakers like Ford began producing their own models, such as the 1937 Ford, marking a shift toward broader accessibility. Post-World War II innovations propelled station wagons to prominence as family vehicles during the baby boom era. In 1946, the Willys Jeep Station Wagon became the first mass-produced all-steel model, followed by the 1949 Plymouth Suburban, which made affordable, practical wagons available to the middle class and helped the style capture up to 17% of the U.S. car market by the late 1950s. The 1950s and 1960s saw peak popularity, with full-size luxury variants like the 1955 Chevrolet Nomad and 1968 Ford Country Squire offering upscale features, two- or four-door configurations, and woodgrain trim, while compact options such as the 1960 Ford Falcon expanded the segment to urban families. These vehicles symbolized suburban expansion, blending sedan comfort with utility for road trips and daily errands. By the 1970s, station wagons faced decline due to the 1973 oil crisis, stricter emissions regulations, and rising fuel costs, which favored smaller, more efficient alternatives. The introduction of minivans in 1984, like the Dodge Caravan and Plymouth Voyager, and SUVs such as the Jeep Cherokee, further eroded their market share by offering greater interior space and perceived ruggedness. Full-size American wagons were largely discontinued by 1996 with the end of the Chevrolet Caprice and Buick Roadmaster lines, though imports and wagon-like crossovers persisted; the Buick Regal TourX in 2020 marked the last traditional station wagon from a U.S. automaker as of 2025, while import models continue to be available in North America. Today, the style endures in Europe and Asia as "estate cars," with modern examples emphasizing performance and all-wheel drive, while in North America, it influences crossover utility vehicles.
